docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text: See installation.md. Verify with phon --version.

docs.title: 2. First .phon file
docs.text:
Create hello.phon:

medium silicon kind photonic;
component wg1 type waveguide length 10.0;
component det1 type detector;

flow main {
    emit wg1 @ phase 0 -> bus;
    detect bus above 0.5 -> out;
    return out;
}

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text: phon run hello.phon

docs.title: 4. Compile to JSON
docs.text: phon compile hello.phon -o hello.json

docs.title: 5. Run all examples
docs.text: phon test

docs.title: Interference
docs.text:
medium silicon kind photonic;
component a type waveguide length 5.0;
component b type waveguide length 5.0;

flow main {
    emit a @ phase 0 -> x;
    emit b @ phase 180 -> y;
    interfere x, y -> out;
    return out;
}

docs.title: Photonic MLP layer
docs.text:
layer l1: 784 -> 128 weights="w1.npy" activation=relu;
layer l2: 128 -> 10 weights="w2.npy" activation=softmax;

flow main {
    band x = 1550.0 @ phase 0;
    propagate x through l1 -> h;
    propagate h through l2 -> out;
    return out;
}

docs.title: Filing Recommendation
docs.text:
Recommended jurisdictions: - EPO (European Patent Office) — primary, since PHON is a European project. - USPTO — secondary, for US market coverage. - PCT — international filing within 12 months of priority date.

Recommended patent type: - Utility patent covering the method and system. - Optional design patent for the DSL syntax (less common but possible in the US).

Prior art to search (initial): - "Phononic computing" academic reviews, 2023-2025 - US 2020/008976 A1 (phononic logic devices) - US 2019/012345 A1 (photonic circuit design languages) - Any patents assigned to Intel / GlobalFoundries / imec on "phononic integrated circuits"

docs.title: Technical Description
docs.text:
Title of Invention: Method and System for Phononic Data Compression and Transmission

Applicant: (to be completed)

Inventor(s): (to be completed)

Priority Date: 2026-10-30

docs.title: 1. Technical Field
docs.text: The invention relates to the field of phononic (acoustic wave) computing and integrated circuit design. Specifically, it relates to a high-level declarative programming language and compiler methodology for designing, simulating, verifying, and deploying phononic integrated circuits for data compression and high-bandwidth signal transmission.

docs.title: 2.1 Prior Art
docs.text:
Phononic computing uses acoustic waves in a solid medium as a data carrier, analogous to photonics using light. Potential advantages include:

  • Lower energy per operation
  • Compatibility with standard CMOS fabrication (GHz-range acoustic waves)
  • Strong nonlinear effects that can be exploited for logic
  • Compact wave confinement in phononic crystals

However, the design of phononic circuits suffers from several deficiencies:

(a) Lack of high-level abstraction. Designers must specify circuits at the physical layer (geometry, material, waveguide dimensions) using finite element or finite difference time domain (FDTD) simulation tools. A 1000x1000 FDTD simulation requires ~700 ms per run, making design-space exploration (DSE) with thousands of variants impractical.

(b) No declarative language for logical behavior. There is no standard way to express "an AND gate as constructive interference" or "a memory cell as a resonator with capture/read" at a level above the physics.

(c) Verification requires full-wave simulation. Confirming that a proposed design performs AND logic requires running full-wave FDTD, which we measured at 24,092x slower than our proposed approach for logical verification.

(d) No standard pipeline from source to hardware. A designer has no path from "I want a register that stores 0xB5" to a deployable artifact (ONNX model, C header, or GDS layout).

docs.title: 2.2 Deficiencies Addressed by the Invention
docs.text:
The invention addresses the above by providing:

  1. A declarative DSL (PHON) with a three-level architecture: Medium (physical environment), Components (resonators, waveguides, detectors, compressors, channels), and Flow (functional operations like emit, interfere, capture, compress, transmit, for).

  2. A compiler pipeline (lexer -> LALR parser -> semantic analyzer -> JSON emitter) that translates PHON source into a machine-checkable hardware description.

  3. A physics-consistent simulator based on idealized wave interference that executes the emitted JSON at 27,467 simulations/sec on CPU (vs. FDTD's 697 ms per simulation).

  4. A compression mechanism in which a phononic resonator array reduces carrier frequency by a configurable ratio (freq_out = freq_in / ratio), enabling dense multichannel encoding.

  5. A transmission mechanism in which a phononic waveguide channel transmits at a rate proportional to channel bandwidth (speed = bandwidth * 100 Gbps).

  6. A machine learning surrogate trained on PHON-generated (input, output) pairs, achieving R^2 = 1.0000 with a Random Forest, and deployable as ONNX or C.

docs.title: 3.1 The PHON Language
docs.text:
PHON is a declarative domain-specific language with three syntactic levels:

  • Medium block: declares the physical substrate (e.g., silicon-on-insulator, LiNbO3), global temperature, and material parameters.
  • Component declarations: typed blocks for resonator, waveguide, detector, compressor, channel, each with physical parameters (frequency, Q factor, bandwidth, ratio).
  • Flow block: imperative-style operations that describe the intended signal path: emit, interfere, detect, capture, read, compress, transmit, for loops, and if conditionals.

Example (AND gate via constructive interference): medium silicon { temperature: 300K; }

resonator r1 { freq: 5GHz; q: 500; } resonator r2 { freq: 5GHz; q: 500; } detector d1 { threshold: 1.5; }

flow main { emit r1 at 5GHz -> amp 2.0; emit r2 at 5GHz -> amp 2.0; interfere r1 r2 -> d1; detect d1; }

text

docs.title: 3.2 Compiler Pipeline
docs.text:
The pipeline is:

  1. Lexer: tokenizes PHON source into a token stream.
  2. Parser: LALR(1) grammar in Lark. Cached (lru_cache) - 0.001 ms for repeated parses.
  3. Semantic analysis: checks for duplicate identifiers, unresolved references, out-of-range values (ratio > 0, bandwidth > 0, for loop bounds), and physical consistency (detector required before detect, etc.).
  4. Emitter: serializes the AST to a JSON hardware description with named operators preserved (->, .., ==, etc.).
  5. Simulator: interprets the JSON and produces a vector of outputs (logic bits, compressed frequencies, transmission rates).

docs.title: 3.3 Compression and Transmission
docs.text:
Compression: A compressor component takes a ratio parameter. A compress(src) at freq -> dst operation emits a signal at freq / ratio into dst. This models the physics of parametric frequency division in a nonlinear acoustic medium, or a divide-by-N resonator array.

Transmission: A channel component takes a bandwidth parameter (in GHz). A transmit(src) via ch -> dst operation transports the signal at bandwidth * 100 Gbps.

Physical interpretation: The compression mechanism reduces frequency, allowing more channels in the same acoustic band. The transmission mechanism scales bandwidth to throughput, matching Shannon's capacity law up to a proportionality constant.

docs.title: 3.4 Machine Learning Surrogate
docs.text:
PHON can generate labeled training data at 89,631 samples/sec by running the simulator over a grid of design parameters. A Random Forest or Neural Network trained on this data achieves R^2 = 1.0000 and can be exported to:

  • ONNX (phon_model.onnx) - for C#/C++/Web deployment
  • C header (phon_model.h) - for microcontrollers (~48 KB)
  • Pickle (.pkl) - for Python reuse

The surrogate provides ~321x speedup over the simulator at inference.

docs.title: 3.5 REST API
docs.text: A FastAPI microservice (api_onnx.py) exposes POST /predict, GET /health, and GET /benchmark endpoints, enabling cloud-native integration of the invention into larger design flows.

docs.title: 4.1 Language Grammar (EBNF summary)
docs.text:
program := medium_decl component* flow_block medium_decl := "medium" IDENT "{" param* "}" component := COMPONENT_TYPE IDENT "{" param* "}" COMPONENT_TYPE := "resonator" | "waveguide" | "detector" | "compressor" | "channel" param := IDENT ":" value ";" flow_block := "flow" IDENT "{" flow_stmt* "}" flow_stmt := emit_stmt | interfere_stmt | detect_stmt | capture_stmt | read_stmt | compress_stmt | transmit_stmt | for_stmt | if_stmt | let_stmt | return_stmt emit_stmt := "emit" IDENT "at" NUMBER "GHz" "->" "amp" NUMBER ";" interfere_stmt := "interfere" IDENT IDENT "->" IDENT ";" detect_stmt := "detect" IDENT ";" capture_stmt := "capture" IDENT "from" IDENT ";" read_stmt := "read" IDENT "from" IDENT ";" compress_stmt := "compress" "(" IDENT ")" "at" NUMBER "->" IDENT ";" transmit_stmt := "transmit" "(" IDENT ")" "via" IDENT "->" IDENT ";" for_stmt := "for" IDENT "from" NUMBER "to" NUMBER "{" flow_stmt* "}"

text

docs.title: 4.2 Simulator Physics
docs.text:
Interference: For two resonators with amplitudes A1, A2 and phases phi1, phi2, the resulting intensity at a detector is: I = A1^2 + A2^2 + 2A1A2*cos(phi1 - phi2)

text

Destructive interference (phi1 - phi2 = pi) yields I = (A1 - A2)^2; constructive (phi1 = phi2) yields I = (A1 + A2)^2. The detector threshold (default 1.5) determines whether the bit reads 0 or 1.

Memory: A resonator with capture from src stores the current amplitude as its internal state. read from m returns a snapshot (not a reference), allowing independent reads.

Compression: freq_out = freq_in / ratio.

Transmission: speed = bandwidth * 100 Gbps.

docs.title: 4.3 Performance Characteristics
docs.text: Operation This invention Baseline (FDTD) Speedup Logical verification 0.029 ms (cached) 697 ms 24,092x Design-space exploration 27,467 sims/sec ~1.4 sims/sec 19,600x ML data generation 89,631 samples/sec N/A - ML inference 6.46M pred/sec - 321x vs simulator Parser (uncached) 2.37 ms 56.5 ms (Earley) 24x

docs.title: 5. Advantages
docs.text:
1. Abstraction: Logic-level semantics decoupled from physical layout.
  2. Speed: 24,000x faster than full-wave verification.
  3. Automation: A complete pipeline from source code to ONNX/C deployable artifact.
  4. Portability: Surrogate models run on edge devices (microcontrollers) via generated C.
  5. Extensibility: New component types (compressors, channels) are added at the grammar level with minimal changes to downstream stages.

docs.title: 6. Industrial Applicability
docs.text:
The invention is applicable to:

  • Design of phononic filters, multiplexers, and delay lines for 5G/6G RF front-ends.
  • Compact data compression for embedded sensor networks.
  • High-throughput short-reach interconnects (>100 Gbps per channel).
  • Rapid prototyping of phononic logic gates for post-CMOS computing.

docs.title: Draft Claims (Preliminary)
docs.text: Note: These are preliminary claims for review by a patent attorney. Claims are drafted in a hybrid style (US + EPO friendly) and require refinement by counsel before filing.

docs.title: Independent Claims
docs.text:
Claim 1. A computer-implemented method for compiling a declarative phononic circuit description, the method comprising:

(a) receiving a source program in a declarative phononic orchestration notation (PHON) language, the source program comprising at least one medium declaration, a plurality of component declarations, and at least one flow block;

(b) tokenizing the source program into a token stream;

(c) parsing the token stream using a LALR(1) parser to produce an abstract syntax tree (AST), wherein the parser is cached so that repeated parses of the same source produce an identical AST in constant time;

(d) performing semantic analysis on the AST, the semantic analysis comprising at least: (i) checking for duplicate component identifiers, (ii) resolving all identifier references in flow statements to declared components, (iii) validating that numeric parameters satisfy physical constraints (ratio > 0, bandwidth > 0, frequency > 0), and (iv) verifying that all detector references are preceded by detector declarations;

(e) serializing the AST into a machine-readable hardware description format, the serialization preserving operator tokens including directional arrows, range operators, and equality operators;

(f) executing the hardware description with a physics-consistent simulator that computes at least one output selected from: (i) a logic bit from constructive or destructive interference, (ii) a compressed output frequency equal to an input frequency divided by a compression ratio, and (iii) a transmission rate equal to a channel bandwidth multiplied by a predefined throughput constant.

Claim 2. The method of claim 1, wherein the component declarations are selected from the group consisting of: resonator, waveguide, detector, compressor, and channel.

Claim 3. The method of claim 1, wherein the compression ratio is a parameter of a compressor component, and the compressed output frequency is computed as freq_in / ratio.

Claim 4. The method of claim 1, wherein the transmission rate is computed as bandwidth_GHz * 100 Gbps.

Claim 5. The method of claim 1, further comprising training a machine learning surrogate model on a dataset of (input parameters, simulator output) pairs generated by the physics-consistent simulator, and exporting the trained model to a portable format selected from: ONNX, a C language header, or a pickle file.

Claim 6. The method of claim 5, wherein the surrogate model is served via an HTTP REST API exposing endpoints for single prediction, batch prediction, health check, and performance benchmarking.

docs.title: Dependent Claims
docs.text:
Claim 7. The method of claim 1, wherein the flow block comprises a for loop statement with explicit lower and upper bounds, and the semantic analysis verifies that the bounds are integers and that the lower bound is less than or equal to the upper bound.

Claim 8. The method of claim 1, wherein the flow block comprises a capture statement that stores the current amplitude of a source component into a target resonator, and a read statement that retrieves a snapshot of the stored value.

Claim 9. The method of claim 1, wherein the physics-consistent simulator computes interference intensity according to I = A1^2 + A2^2 + 2*A1*A2*cos(phi1 - phi2) and compares the result against a configurable detector threshold.

Claim 10. The method of claim 1, wherein the parser is configured to fall back from LALR(1) to Earley parsing for source files that are not LALR-parseable.

Claim 11. A system for phononic circuit design, comprising: a processor; a memory storing instructions that cause the processor to execute the method of claim 1; and a network interface configured to expose the method as a REST API endpoint.

Claim 12. A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by a processor, cause the processor to execute the method of claim 1.

docs.title: Notes for Attorney
docs.text:
• Novelty argument: The combination of (a) declarative DSL with three-level architecture, (b) LALR + caching pipeline, and (c) physics-consistent simulator that computes compression and transmission as first-class operations, is not disclosed in the prior art we are aware of.
  • Inventive step argument: Existing phononic design tools are either full-wave (FDTD) or rely on SPICE-like netlists. PHON abstracts at the logic level while remaining physically grounded (interference formula).
  • Claim 1 preamble: Consider broadening to "declarative hardware description language" if counsel advises.
  • Claim 5: The ML surrogate may be pursued as a separate divisional if the examiner objects.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text:
Title: Method and System for Phononic Data Compression and Transmission

A method and system for compiling and simulating declarative phononic circuit descriptions. A source program in a domain-specific language (PHON) is tokenized, parsed via a LALR(1) parser, semantically validated, and serialized into a JSON hardware description. A physics-consistent simulator then executes the description, computing logic bits from constructive or destructive interference, compressed frequencies via a freq_out = freq_in / ratio relation, and transmission rates via speed = bandwidth * 100 Gbps. The invention is 24,092x faster than full-wave FDTD verification for logical checks, enables design-space exploration at 27,467 simulations/sec, and provides a machine-learning surrogate (R^2 = 1.0000) deployable as ONNX or C for edge and cloud integration. The pipeline is exposed as a FastAPI REST microservice.

(Word count: ~130 — within the 150-word USPTO / 150-word EPO limit)

docs.text:
FIG. 1 — System architecture. Three horizontal layers: Medium (silicon / LiNbO3 with temperature annotation), Components (five boxes: resonator, waveguide, detector, compressor, channel), Flow (six arrows: emit, interfere, capture, compress, transmit, for-loop). Arrows point downward from Flow to Components to Medium.

FIG. 2 — Compiler pipeline. Left-to-right flow: Source file .phon -> Lexer (token stream icon) -> Parser LALR (tree icon) -> Semantic analyzer (magnifier + checkmark) -> Emitter (curly-brace icon JSON) -> Simulator (wave icon) -> Output vector.

FIG. 3 — Physics of interference. Two amplitude vectors A1, A2 originating from a common point, with angle delta_phi = phi1 - phi2 between them. A dashed resultant vector of magnitude sqrt(A1^2 + A2^2 + 2A1A2*cos(delta_phi)). Two inset plots: (a) delta_phi = 0, showing constructive sum; (b) delta_phi = pi, showing cancellation.

FIG. 4 — Compression mechanism. A block labeled "Compressor (ratio R)" with input arrow labeled "freq_in" and output arrow labeled "freq_out = freq_in / R". Below: two frequency-domain magnitude plots, before (peak at freq_in) and after (peak at freq_in / R).

FIG. 5 — Transmission mechanism. A block labeled "Channel (bandwidth B GHz)" with input pulse and output pulse train. Annotated: "speed = B * 100 Gbps". Below: a time-domain plot of pulses with rate labeled.

FIG. 6 — ML surrogate pipeline. Five boxes connected left-to-right: "PHON simulator (N samples)" -> "Feature engineering" -> "Random Forest training" -> "ONNX export" -> three parallel deployment boxes: "REST API (FastAPI)", "C header (MCU)", "ONNX Runtime (C#/Web)".

FIG. 7 — Performance comparison. Bar chart on log scale. Three bars: "FDTD 697 ms/run", "PHON (cached) 0.029 ms/run", "ML inference 1.55 us/batch". Annotations: "24,092x" over FDTD bar, "321x" over PHON bar.

FIG. 8 — Register8 example. Eight resonator circles labeled r0..r7 (top row), eight parallel waveguides labeled bus0..bus7 (middle row), eight detector squares labeled d0..d7 (bottom row). An arrow labeled "capture 0xB5" enters from the left, and an arrow labeled "read back 0xB5" exits to the right.

docs.text:
PHON is publicly released on GitHub at https://github.com/Popisone/PHON

Release timeline: - v0.4.0 released 2026-10-29 (compressor, channel, compress, transmit, REST API, C export, ONNX) - v0.5.0 released 2026-10-29 (for loops, ONNX Runtime API) - v0.6.0-docs released 2026-10-30 (this patent documentation)

JURISDICTION ANALYSIS:

United States (USPTO): - Grace period: 12 months from inventor own disclosure (35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(A)) - Status: FILING DEADLINE = 2027-10-29 - Recommendation: viable, must file before 2027-10-29

European Patent Office (EPO): - Grace period: NONE for inventor own publication (Art. 55 EPC exceptions do NOT cover ordinary publication) - Status: NOVELTY LIKELY DESTROYED for all matter publicly disclosed 2026-10-29 - Recommendation: NOT viable for the core invention as of 2026-10-29

PCT (Patent Cooperation Treaty): - Follows national rules for grace period after entering national phase - Status: depends on designated states

STRATEGY RECOMMENDATION: 1. File USPTO utility application before 2027-10-29 2. Focus claims on novel matter NOT in v0.4.0 / v0.5.0 releases (v0.6+ features) 3. Consider defensive publication strategy for EPO 4. Consider trade secret for future developments

docs.title: 1. Prior Art Categories
docs.text:
The invention should be compared against prior art in:

1.1 Phononic computing hardware - Phononic crystal logic gates - Acoustic wave interference devices - Surface acoustic wave (SAW) filters and multiplexers

1.2 Design automation for wave-based computing - Photonic circuit design languages (GDSII, IPKISS, Luceda) - Phononic / mechanical circuit design tools - SPICE-like simulators for non-electrical domains

1.3 DSL and compiler design for hardware - Hardware description languages (Verilog, VHDL, Chisel, MyHDL) - High-level synthesis (HLS) tools - Domain-specific languages for analog design

1.4 Machine learning surrogates for physics simulation - Neural network surrogates for FDTD / FEM - Gaussian process regression for design space exploration

1.5 Data compression and transmission in wave-based systems - Photonic data compression - Acoustic data transmission protocols

docs.title: 5. Novelty Analysis (Preliminary)
docs.text:
What we believe is novel about PHON (subject to prior art search):

A. Three-level declarative DSL (Medium / Components / Flow) for phononic circuits B. Physics-consistent simulator for logic verification at 24,092x speedup vs FDTD C. Compression mechanism (freq_out = freq_in / ratio) as first-class language primitive D. Transmission mechanism (speed = bandwidth * 100 Gbps) as first-class language primitive E. Machine learning surrogate with R^2 = 1.0000 trained on PHON-generated data F. Unified pipeline: source -> LALR parser -> JSON -> simulator -> ONNX/C

What is likely NOT novel (publicly disclosed before or widely known): - Wave interference as a logic primitive (well-known in photonics) - DSLs for hardware description (many exist) - ML surrogates for physics simulation (many exist)

Strongest claims are likely A, C, D, and F.

docs.title: detect
docs.text: Detect a signal above a threshold. Returns 1 if |signal| >= threshold, else 0.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: detect <signal> above <threshold> -> <variable>;

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
emit wg1 @ phase 0 -> bus;
detect bus above 0.5 -> out;  # out = 1

emit wg2 @ phase 180 -> dark;
detect dark above 0.5 -> out2;  # out2 = 0

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Threshold comparison uses >=. A value exactly equal to the threshold returns 1.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• emit
  • interfere

docs.title: flow
docs.text: Main execution block. Each PHON program has exactly one flow main.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
flow main {
    <statements>
}

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
medium silicon kind photonic;
component wg1 type waveguide length 10.0;
component det1 type detector;

flow main {
    emit wg1 @ phase 0 -> bus;
    detect bus above 0.5 -> out;
    return out;
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The flow main block is executed sequentially. Variables are scoped to the block.

docs.title: interfere
docs.text: Interfere two signals. The result amplitude is |a + b|.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: interfere <sig1>, <sig2> -> <variable>;

docs.title: Constructive interference
docs.text:
emit a @ phase 0 -> x;
emit b @ phase 0 -> y;
interfere x, y -> out;  # out = 2.0

docs.title: Destructive interference
docs.text:
emit a @ phase 0 -> x;
emit b @ phase 180 -> y;
interfere x, y -> out;  # out = 0.0

docs.title: Physics
docs.text:
The interference uses the complex amplitude sum:

out = |exp(i*phase1) + exp(i*phase2)|

docs.text:
• emit
  • detect

docs.title: layer
docs.text: Neural network layer. Defines a linear projection + activation.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: layer <name>: <in> -> <out> weights="<path>" activation=<kind>;

docs.title: Activation kinds
docs.text:
• relu
  • sigmoid
  • tanh
  • softmax
  • linear

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
layer l1: 784 -> 128 weights="w1.npy" activation=relu;
layer l2: 128 -> 10 weights="w2.npy" activation=softmax;

flow main {
    band x = 1550.0 @ phase 0;
    propagate x through l1 -> h;
    propagate h through l2 -> out;
    return out;
}

docs.title: medium
docs.text: Declare the physical medium for the circuit.

docs.title: mzi
docs.text: Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Applies a 2x2 unitary to two modes.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: mzi theta=<value> phi=<value> on <in1>, <in2> -> <out1>, <out2>;

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description theta float (radians) Beamsplitter angle phi float (radians) Phase shift

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
component a type waveguide length 1.0;
component b type waveguide length 1.0;

flow main {
    emit a @ phase 0 -> x;
    emit b @ phase 0 -> y;
    mzi theta=0.7854 phi=0.0 on x, y -> x_out, y_out;
    return x_out;
}

docs.title: Execution model
docs.text:
1. All medium and component declarations are evaluated first.
  2. The flow main block is executed sequentially.
  3. Variables are scoped to the flow main block.
  4. return exits the flow with the given value.

docs.title: Types
docs.text: PHON is dynamically typed. Values can be: - Numbers (float) - Strings - Signals (complex amplitude) - Vectors (for neural networks)

docs.title: Signal model
docs.text:
A signal s has a complex amplitude A * exp(i * phase).

  • emit creates a signal with amplitude 1.0 at the given phase.
  • interfere computes |s1 + s2|.
  • detect returns 1.0 if |s| >= threshold, else 0.0.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
• Phase: degrees (0-360)
  • Length: arbitrary units (typically mm or um)
  • Frequency: GHz or THz
  • Loss: dB/m

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning PHON001 Syntax error PHON002 Undefined variable PHON003 Type mismatch PHON004 Dimension mismatch PHON005 Unknown component PHON006 Missing flow main PHON007 Runtime simulation error

docs.title: Tutorial 1: Your First Photon
docs.text: Time: 5 minutes.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Create a simple waveguide circuit, emit a photon, detect it.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the file
docs.text:
Save as hello.phon:

medium silicon kind photonic;
component wg1 type waveguide length 10.0;
component det1 type detector;

flow main {
    emit wg1 @ phase 0 -> bus;
    detect bus above 0.5 -> out;
    return out;
}

docs.title: Step 2: Run it
docs.text:
phon run hello.phon

Expected output:

# hello.phon
out: 1.0

docs.title: Step 3: Understand
docs.text:
1. medium silicon kind photonic - declares a photonic circuit
  2. component wg1 type waveguide - a 10-unit waveguide
  3. emit wg1 @ phase 0 - emits a photon at phase 0
  4. detect bus above 0.5 - detects if |signal| >= 0.5
  5. return out - returns the result

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Tutorial 2: MZI Mesh

docs.title: Tutorial 2: MZI Mesh
docs.text: Time: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Build a 2x2 Mach-Zehnder interferometer and see interference.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the file
docs.text:
Save as mzi.phon:

medium silicon kind photonic;
component a type waveguide length 1.0;
component b type waveguide length 1.0;

flow main {
    emit a @ phase 0 -> x;
    emit b @ phase 0 -> y;
    interfere x, y -> out;
    return out;
}

docs.title: Step 2: Run it
docs.text:
phon run mzi.phon

Expected: out: 2.0 (constructive interference)

docs.title: Step 3: Try destructive
docs.text:
Change emit b @ phase 0 to emit b @ phase 180. Run again.

Expected: out: 0.0 (destructive interference)

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Tutorial 3: Reck Decomposition

docs.title: Tutorial 3: Reck Decomposition
docs.text: Time: 15 minutes.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Decompose an arbitrary 4x4 unitary into a Reck MZI mesh.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Reck 1994 showed that any U(N) can be decomposed into a triangular mesh of MZIs.

docs.title: Step 1: Generate the mesh
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import unitary_group
from phon.reck import reck_decompose, ops_to_phon

U = unitary_group.rvs(4, random_state=42)
ops = reck_decompose(U)
phon_code = ops_to_phon(ops, n=4)
print(phon_code)

docs.title: Step 2: Save and run
docs.text:
Save the printed code as reck.phon, then:

phon run reck.phon

docs.title: Step 3: Verify
docs.text:
The simulator output should match the original U up to 1e-14.

See examples/reck_full_4x4.phon for a working example.
